text.p: One of the last hopes of survival for bankrupt Dutch planemaker Fokker vanished on Tuesday as the South Korean government ruled out the prospect of a takeover by a consortium led by Samsung Aerospace.
The following is a chronology of the main events in the history of Fokker, one of the world's oldest aviation marques.
* 1912 -- Anthony Fokker begins building planes for German army, including fighters like the Fokker triplane favoured by the Red Baron in World War One.
* 1919 -- Fokker established as a commercial company.
* 1928 -- Fokker is world's biggest planemaker, designing revolutionary aircraft like the Fokker IV which made aviation history with a coast-to-coast crossing of the U.S. in 1922.
* 1957 -- Fokker launches the famous F27 Fokker Friendship turboprop, still in service 30 years later.
* 1969 -- Fokker enters cooperation pact with German aerospace manufacturer VFW, but the relationship is tense from the start.
* 1980 -- Fokker and VFW go their separate ways.
* 1981 -- Fokker and McDonnell Douglas of the U.S. decide to work together.
* 1983 -- Fokker launches plans to build the F50 and F100 jets at a development cost of 1.6 billion guilders ($918 million).
* 1985/86 -- F50 and F100 make their first flights.
* 1986 -- Fokker shares hit a high of 99.50 guilders on optimism about F50 and F100 programmes.
* 1987 -- Dutch state saves Fokker from threat of bankruptcy caused by spiralling development costs, taking 49 percent equity stake in company.
* 1990 -- Fokker recovers, posts profit of 83 million guilders.
* 1991 -- Fokker sets out to find new industry partner.
* 1993 -- Daimler-Benz AG 's DASA unit agrees to pay 686 million guilders for a 51 percent stake in Fokker.
* 1994 -- Fokker announces first of a string of heavy losses and sacks 1,100 of its 13,000 workforce.
* JULY 1994 -- Dutch government and DASA pump an additional one billion guilders of fresh capital into the company.
* AUGUST 1995 -- Fokker posts record first-half loss of 651 million guilders. Shares slump to 5.60 guilders.
* SEPTEMBER 1995 -- Two major shareholders, DASA and Dutch state, refuse Fokker request for another 2.3 billion guilders.
* JANUARY 1996
-- Daimler Benz cuts off financial support. Dutch state says will explore other rescue options.
-- Canada's Bombardier surfaces as possible saviour.
-- Dutch state offers 255 million guilder credit line to keep Fokker alive while it looks for buyer.
* FEBRUARY 1996
-- Fokker says in talks with five serious potential buyers (Samsung, British Aerospace, France's Aerospatiale, Taiwanese government and Bombardier)
-- Bombardier says no longer interested.
* MARCH 1996 -- Fokker declares bankruptcy at three core units. Non-core businesses such as space systems, electronics and aircraft services live on, but need new partners.
* APRIL 1996 -- Fokker says Samsung no longer interested in bidding for company.
* JUNE 1996 -- Fokker remains in production after Dutch airline KLM orders seven 70-seat aircraft.
* JULY 1996 -- Dutch industrial systems group Stork buys Fokker Aviation, Fokker's parts, maintenance and special services unit.
* AUGUST 1996 -- Samsung re-emerges as possible buyer.
* SEPTEMBER 1996 -- Samsung begins due diligence procedures.
* OCTOBER 1996 -- Samsung hands Fokker business plan to Dutch Economics Ministry.
-- Samsung, Economics Ministry delegates begin talks on Fokker re-launch.
-- Administrators tell staff that rescue deadline is end-October.
* NOVEMBER 5 1996 -- Dutch government expects decision on Samsung takeover "within days".
* NOVEMBER 13 1996 -- Samsung invites Korea's Daewoo and Hyundai to take part in Fokker rescue.

* NOVEMBER 28 1996 -- Court-appointed administrators at Fokker said they had ended possible rescue talks with Samsung afer Shorts, one of Fokker's suppliers, said it would no longer supply wings for Fokker aircraft.
* DECEMBER 20 1996 -- Russian plane-maker Yakovlev, mooted as a possible buyer in August, says it is still optimistic that it can purchase Fokker.
* DECEMBER 31 1996 -- South Korean government informs Dutch government that it is ruling out a takeover by the consortium led by Samsung Aerospace.
